\section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:eval}

\subsection{Setup}

Three evaluators are used and never confused. A deterministic \emph{mock} obeys
the same physics as the elimination bounds, which is what makes a disagreement
between the search and an exhaustive oracle meaningful; it is not a
performance model and no figure produced by it is a measurement.
\emph{LLMServingSim} with an analytical network backend is the real simulator.
\emph{Hardware} is an eight-GPU node, joined for the inter-node measurements by
a second node of the same accelerator over one InfiniBand link; every raw file
records the accelerator serial numbers it ran on. Every table carries its
provenance in the caption.

Every fixture in the accompanying repository is fictional and says so in its
header, with three exceptions. The descriptions of the eight-GPU node and of
the two-node pair are generated from the microbenchmarks' own raw files, so
that each figure marked as measured is traceable to a file recording the
node's serials, the process binding, the load average and which other
processes held a GPU; figures not measured there are marked as placeholders.
The third is a holdout derived from the eight-GPU description by one assumed
reservation, which is a variation of the topology and not a measurement.

The success criteria, the numeric limits, and the interval a threshold was
chosen from were registered before the corresponding experiment ran, in the
manner of a preregistration~\cite{nosek2018}, and the registration is
append-only. Where a limit was derived from a measurement, the
runs it was derived from are named and excluded from the set that tests it.
Analyses added after a result was known---the hardware re-prediction of
Section~\ref{sec:eval-hw} among them---are labelled post hoc wherever they
appear, and none of them tests a registered prediction.

\paragraph{Provenance tags} Every table and figure of results carries one of
three tags in its caption, and the tag is what its numbers are; the reuse
table, which holds no result, is marked as not a measurement. \sourcetag{MOCK}: the mock
predictor. These are not performance numbers. The mock obeys the same physics
as the elimination bounds, which is what makes a disagreement with the oracle
meaningful, but no figure so tagged is a measurement or a simulation of any
hardware. \sourcetag{REAL SIM}: LLMServingSim. Simulated, not measured. The
figures are the simulator's output under a cache the artifact names, and no
hardware was run. \sourcetag{REAL HARDWARE}: measured, on nodes whose serials
the raw files record; a percentile is the median of the repetitions, with
their range, and a single trial is not reported as a measurement.

\subsection{Correctness under the real simulator}

% claim: C10
% claim: C13
Under the real simulator, does the search eliminate a feasible placement or
fold two that the oracle prices apart? No, among the placements the simulator
judged: on all three fixtures both correctness numbers are zero
(\texttt{false\_infeasible} is \egthreeFalseInfAbcde{} on the largest). The
first run was complete on none of them; re-run once the missing profile was
measured, both toy fixtures are complete and both numbers stay zero.

% claim: C10
% claim: C11
% claim: C12
\input{e_g3_real_sim_oracle}

Table~\ref{tab:e_g3_real_sim_oracle} reports the search against an exhaustive
oracle, both driven by LLMServingSim.

% claim: C13
The \texttt{complete} column above is the first run's, and the failures in it
have two established causes. % claim: C14
On the toy corpora every failure was a missing profile: no measurement existed
for that tensor-parallel degree on that hardware, and the simulator refused
rather than extrapolating. With the profile measured, a re-run judged every
placement on both: each verdict the first run reached was unchanged, and some
formerly unjudged placements proved feasible, which counting failures as
rejections would have eliminated unnoticed. On the heterogeneous fixture
\egthreeUnjudgedLab{} of the \egthreeEmbeddingsLab{} placements still return
no verdict, each a decode instance running out of KV mid-run---all of them
prefill on the larger device feeding decode on the smaller, with the reverse
direction succeeding. They remain \texttt{unknown\_measurement}, not
infeasible: a crash is not a verdict, and on that fixture the correctness claim
is about the placements the simulator judged.

Against what it saved, the compression is cheap (full timing table in the
artifact). On the largest fixture, \egthreeSimOracleAbcde~seconds
of oracle simulation become \egthreeSimProposedAbcde, a saving of
\egthreeSavingAbcde~seconds with the hashing, the isomorphism checks and the
bound evaluation all charged against the compression rather than ignored.

The compression ratio is a property of the graph and not of the evaluator: it
agrees to four decimals between the mock and the real simulator on every shared
fixture.

\subsection{Contribution A: the boundary in the signature}

% claim: C24
Does dropping the shared boundary from the signature produce a mis-merge? Yes,
on the counterexample pair it exists for, under a threshold derived from the
oracle; across the toy corpus under the fixed tight specification no arm can
show one.

\input{e_g7_ablation}

% claim: C24
Across the toy corpus (Table~\ref{tab:e_g7_ablation}), under
the fixed tight specification, every arm reports no mis-merged pairs,
\texttt{no\_boundary} included, even where it folds more: the placements
\texttt{no\_boundary} folds together there are all infeasible, so the oracle
cannot tell a wrong fold from a right one. The
claim is tested on the counterexample pair it is about. There, with
\texttt{no\_boundary} and every other label retained, the two placements that
differ only in which uplink they cross are folded into one representative and
the oracle prices them apart, a mis-merged pair. The full relation keeps them
as two representatives and mis-merges nothing
(Table~\ref{tab:e_g7_ablation_4}).

\input{e_g7_ablation_4}

The threshold that decides ``prices them apart'' is derived from the oracle's
own distribution, and is stated with the count, which depends on it.

\subsection{Search quality}

% claim: C5
% claim: C6
% claim: C32
Does the search retrieve more feasible placements than HeteroPilot's surrogate
at the same budget? Only in part: in-sample at every $K$ tried, on the two
holdouts only at $K = 16$, and not on the hardware-derived holdout.

% claim: C5
% claim: C6
% claim: C32
\begin{figure}[t]\centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{topk_holdout.pdf}
  \caption{Feasible recall against the simulation budget, both arms, on the holdout fixtures~\sourcetag{MOCK}. The oracle's level is the dotted line. At $K=4$ the graph search ties on one holdout and is behind on the other, which the curve shows without the reader comparing two rows.}
  \label{fig:topk}
\end{figure}

% claim: C5
% claim: C6
% claim: C32
Figure~\ref{fig:topk} and the artifact's tables report feasible recall against HeteroPilot's~\cite{heteropilot} surrogate top-$K$ under a
specification whose SLOs bind. The toy corpus is the set of diagnosis fixtures the
ranker correction was made on, so it is in-sample. On it this search reaches
higher recall at every $K$ tried (on \texttt{graph-toy-abcde} at $K = 16$,
\egonebRecallGraphAbcde{} against the surrogate's \egonebRecallSurrogateAbcde{}). On the two holdouts it is higher at $K = 16$ and
level at $K = 8$; at $K = 4$ it ties on one and trails on the other. On the hardware-derived holdout below it
is lower at $K = 16$.

The baseline is scored generously and deliberately so. It ranks and judges
templates rather than placements, so it cannot name which devices a candidate
occupies; one verdict is therefore credited to every placement of the template
it judged.

% claim: C25
% claim: C26
\input{e_g7_holdout}

% claim: C26
% claim: C32
Table~\ref{tab:e_g7_holdout} reports both holdouts, fixed before the scaling
grid ran. On the synthetic one, \egsevenHoldoutEmbeddings{} embeddings compress
to \egsevenHoldoutReps{} representatives, both correctness numbers are zero,
and recall at the registered operating point is higher than the surrogate's.
The second holdout is the hardware fixture with one PCIe-port reservation
altered (\texttt{port-gpu0}).

\textbf{On it the registered recall criterion is not met.} The invariant holds
there: nothing feasible was removed and nothing mis-merged. But at the
registered budget HeteroPilot's template-level surrogate retrieves more
feasible placements than this search does. The response was registered before
the run: the ranker was fitted to the diagnosis corpus, and the claim about it
narrows to those fixtures and the synthetic holdout. It is reported as a
failure of the \emph{ranking}, not of the correctness, which is separately
evidenced. The
result file states that the altered reservation is a variation of a topology
assumption rather than a physical claim, together with what it does to the
search: it moves candidates out of the feasible set, and they leave evaluated
and rejected rather than unevaluated.

\subsection{The contention model against the wire}

% claim: C15
Does processor sharing predict measured transfer time? Not on the topology
registered before measuring, where the registered verdict is a failure. On the
intra-node bus, on the declaration the measurements support, it does, up to a
message size above which it is pessimistic.

% claim: C15
% claim: C16
\begin{figure}[t]\centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{contention_error.pdf}
  \caption{Fluid and null error against message size, on the declaration the measurements support~\sourcetag{REAL HARDWARE}. The bidirectional error is near zero from 4 to 64 MiB and rises at 128: an accuracy domain, not a single figure.}
  \label{fig:contention}
\end{figure}

The registered verdict is a \textbf{failure}: on the topology the plan declared before measuring,
processor-sharing is \egfourFluidPlannedSame\,\% out at the median on the
condition it exists for, against \egfourNullPlannedSame\,\% for pricing each
flow alone.

The reason is not the model. Two device pairs believed to share a host bridge
were measured to share nothing: each concurrent copy sustained the full
single-copy rate, and a third process saturating one pair left the other at its
unloaded rate to three digits. Run on the declaration the measurements support,
the same model is \egfourFluidMeasuredSame\,\% out; and on the bidirectional
condition, where the two flows genuinely do share endpoints, it is
\egfourFluidMeasuredBidi\,\% against \egfourNullMeasuredBidi\,\% for the null
model.

Both are reported because they are different corrections: one would rewrite
the model, the other a line of a cluster description. The registered verdict is computed on the registered declaration, and the corrected
figure is not offered in its place.

% claim: C22
% claim: C29
\paragraph{The same question at a second location, with the opposite answer.}
Across an inter-node NIC between two machines, two concurrent streams take
exactly half each: a single stream reaches \egfourNicSingle~Gbit/s and two
reach \egfourNicTwoSame~each. Processor sharing predicts exactly this, and
the intra-node PCIe pairs did not do it.

The model is not right in one place and wrong in another: \emph{which resource
is genuinely shared} is a claim about hardware, settled by measurement at each
location separately, and the model prices whatever it is told to. The
bidirectional case says the same thing twice: the intra-node pair reaches only
a third again as much as a single direction, while the NIC exceeds twice it,
because that wire really is full duplex.

% claim: C31
So does the collective: a two-rank all-reduce reaches \egfourCollNicTwo~GB/s
of bus bandwidth across the NIC against \egfourCollNodeTwo{} inside one node,
so a bandwidth figure is keyed by \emph{where} it was taken as well as by how
many ranks took part. (Flows over two \emph{disjoint} NICs, also registered,
cannot be tested: each machine has one InfiniBand device.)

% claim: C15
The model's accuracy domain has an upper end. Above a message size the hardware
begins overlapping the two directions of one link, the pair exceeds what
processor sharing predicts, and the model becomes pessimistic: it predicts the
transfer about a third slower than measured.
That boundary is stated rather than absorbed into a fitted capacity, which
would not be a measurement.

\subsection{Hardware}
\label{sec:eval-hw}

% claim: C18
% claim: C33
Does the placement matter on hardware, and does the search's registered
verdict follow it? At the load knee, yes: the two tensor-parallel pairs'
median $p99$ time to first token differs \egfiveTtwoOverTone{}x, and with the
registered adapter, which a post-hoc correction below qualifies, the verdict
matches the hardware's at both. It does not at the
four-way group, whose \egfiveReps{} deployments are all predicted met and all
miss.

\input{e_g5_real_hardware}

% claim: C18
Table~\ref{tab:e_g5_real_hardware} reports the recommendation at three
placements, \egfiveReps{} repetitions each, at the load knee of the registered
specification: one tensor-parallel pair on two different pairs of devices, and
a four-way group. \textbf{The same pair's median $p99$ time to first token is
\egfiveTtwoOverTone{}x higher on one wire than on the other}, \egfiveTtwoMedian{}
against \egfiveToneMedian{} ms, with the same model, trace, scheduler knobs,
seed and plan. The ranges do not overlap: the slowest repetition on the
faster wire measured \egfiveToneRangeHi{} ms and the fastest on the slower wire
\egfiveTtwoRangeLo{} ms. Against the latency target the faster wire meets and
the slower misses. The verdict is partly by construction, and the ratio is the
evidence that does not depend on it: the target was registered before the
matrix ran, derived from the faster placement's own pilot $p99$ with a margin
above it, and so sits between the two placements by design. Time per output
token (median $p99$ \egfiveToneTpot{} and \egfiveTtwoTpot{} ms) and goodput
(\egfiveToneGoodput{} and \egfiveTtwoGoodput{} rps) clear their targets at
both, so the latency axis is the one that decides.

HeteroPilot cannot express the difference between those two
placements at all. It names a template, and has no language for the choice
this experiment shows to be decisive.

\input{e_g5_real_hardware_3}

% claim: C33
\textbf{Asked about the placement it is deployed on, with the registered
adapter, the search tells the two pairs apart}---a reading the corrected
adapter below qualifies. Counting independent deployments of the recommendation only
(Table~\ref{tab:e_g5_real_hardware_3}), the verdict matches the hardware's in every one of the \egfiveReps{} repetitions at
both pairs, and in none at the four-way group, where each is a predicted
\emph{met} that the hardware misses. A false \emph{met} is the direction that
matters to a planner, and it is reported as a miss. The table carries two
further rows per repetition that are not further tests of this question. The
feasible-marginal alternative deployed the recommendation's own template at
the same devices, so it is the same configuration measured twice; and the
bound-stress row, a candidate predicted to miss by tens of seconds, agrees
trivially and is taken up below. An earlier harness printed the search's own pick beside every
measurement, so the two pairs looked indistinguishable; that reading was a
harness defect and is withdrawn.

% claim: C34
\textbf{Post hoc, the four-way miss has a candidate cause.} The adapter gave
the simulator a tensor-parallel group's first rank pair's bandwidth only---for
the four-way group, one NVLink pair's capacity, where its measured four-rank
all-reduce is \egfourBusbwFour~GB/s. Every registered prediction used that
figure and every verdict above stands. Corrected and re-simulated, unregistered
and with nothing redeployed, the group's recommendation and closest-miss rows
agree in \egfivePostTthreeReAgree{} of \egfivePostTthreeRows{} (originally
\egfivePostTthreeOrigAgree{}) and its false \emph{met} verdicts fall from
\egfivePostTthreeOrigFp{} to \egfivePostTthreeReFp. The correction is not
free: on the NVLink pair agreement falls from \egfivePostToneOrigAgree{} to
\egfivePostToneReAgree{} of \egfivePostToneRows{}, each new disagreement a
predicted miss the hardware met.

% claim: C36
\textbf{Post hoc, the goodput floor changes the answer only at low load.}
Re-judging the cached predictions at floors from \egfiveFloorLow{} to
\egfiveFloorHigh{} requests per second changes whether a recommendation exists
in \egfiveFloorChanged{} of \egfiveFloorRows{} condition-seeds, all at the low
load, where a floor derived from the hardware's goodput sits above the
simulator's lower prediction of it.

% claim: C35
\textbf{The ratio depends on load.} A widened matrix, registered beforehand,
adds a lower and a higher load and a burstier pattern. The pair's ratio
between the wires is \egfiveWideLowRatio{}x below the knee,
\egfiveTtwoOverTone{}x at it and \egfiveWideHighRatio{}x above, so the claim
is scoped to the knee. The four-way group is predicted to meet its target
everywhere; the hardware meets it only below the knee under the registered
pattern (median \egfiveWideTthreeLow{} ms).

% claim: C19
% claim: C20
\textbf{The lower bound was right, and loose.} The candidate the throughput
bound rejected by the smallest margin, deployed at the floor it was rejected
against, did not reach it, so this one rejection was not wrong on hardware---a
weak test by construction, since a relaxation rejects only what the most
optimistic arithmetic already misses. The bound's ceiling exceeds the capacity
the hardware delivered by more than an order of magnitude: the price of
soundness, on this machine. Its time to first token is predicted optimistic in
most rows, and the causes are not separated.


\subsection{Across two accelerator types}
\label{sec:eval-pd}

% claim: C38
% claim: C39
Do the verdict and the contention model hold when prefill and decode run on
different accelerators? Neither does.

% claim: C38
% claim: C39
\input{e_g8_hetero_pd}

% claim: C38
\textbf{The registered agreement, \egeightAgree{} of \egeightRuns{} runs, is
trivial.} An A40 and an RTX A5000 on two nodes take prefill and decode in turn,
in both directions, at an unqueued load, the KV pulled over GPUDirect by
NIXL~\cite{nixl} (Table~\ref{tab:e_g8_hetero_pd}). Every prediction misses the
goodput floor, which row 4's rule derives from the hardware's goodput while the
simulator predicts less, and every run misses on latency, so both sides read
as misses. On latency alone the verdict agrees in \egeightLatAgree{} of
\egeightRuns{}: the simulator under-predicts $p99$ time to first token in both
directions. With the A5000 decoding, the simulator raised on every candidate at
the selection load, so that direction deploys the other's template mirrored.

% claim: C39
\textbf{The contention model over-predicts on all three inter-node directions
measured}, with measured-to-predicted ratios of \egeightGfiveRatio{} on the
same-accelerator pair (Section~\ref{sec:limits}), \egeightDoneRatio{} with the
A40 sending and \egeightDtwoRatio{} with the A5000 sending. Post hoc and not
registered, a competing flow in place of the reservation gives
\egeightPsGfive{}, \egeightPsDone{} and \egeightPsDtwo{}: it accounts for one
direction only. Why the two directions between the same nodes differ is not
separated here.

% claim: C40
\textbf{KV exhaustion appears in the pilot only.} With the A5000 decoding, the
hardware preempts from \egeightOnset{} requests per second; the simulator
judges the same placement up to \egeightCeiling{} and raises from
\egeightRaises{}. No validation run preempted.
